slot_note: seed ET31 (Connecticut's planning regions replacing its counties; a fixed anti-poverty grant split on a five-vintage poverty average; history rebuilt from towns): world, decision and quantity kept, the pitfall re-found in how the town data describe time
niche: rebuilding a state's annual model-based poverty series on new county-equivalents for a formula grant, the former counties' 2020-2022 years split by town with SNAP counts benchmarked to the survey's five-year town level
answer: Greater Ormsby $1,650,000; Mill River Valley $2,250,000; Tarrow Uplands $330,000; Southern Shore $720,000; Wexport Harbor $2,140,000; Two Rivers $1,860,000; Northern Hills $330,000; Quinnet Valley $1,380,000; Eastern Bays $1,340,000
analyst_test: A strong analyst who reads every file and rule correctly splits each former county's 2020, 2021 and 2022 poverty estimate among its towns by their shares in the Bureau's 2020-2024 five-year release and files Greater Ormsby $1,620,000 and Mill River Valley $2,280,000 (six of nine amounts off); splitting by the year's SNAP recipients instead files Greater Ormsby $1,750,000 and Southern Shore $660,000 (all nine off); reading the release as 2022 and moving it by SNAP files Greater Ormsby $1,680,000; only each town's SNAP recipients that year scaled to its own five-year survey level files the golden.
domain_test: The deciding quantity is each planning region's residents in poverty in 2020 to 2022, years the State Data Center estimated only for the former counties, built the way official statisticians produce annual small-area figures across a break: temporal disaggregation with an indicator benchmarked to the low-frequency level (monthly SNAP recipients by town carry the year's timing, the survey's five-year town count carries the level); with another field's nouns the task loses the model totals, the period-average survey windows and the administrative indicator whose take-up differs by town.

spine.entity: one service delivered to one person by a former county agency

world.geography: United States, an unnamed New England state
world.org_type: the State Data Center, which prepares the Regional Opportunity Fund's allocation for the Office of Policy and Management

driver: A total published only for coarse units in some periods is split across a crossing partition by each fine unit's value that period, estimated by scaling an every-period indicator, whose ratio to the target differs by unit, to the unit's own multi-period average of the target; the multi-period average alone carries moves from later periods into earlier ones and the indicator alone carries its own ratio.
driver_concrete: Each former county's 2020-2022 poverty estimate is split into the planning regions by its towns' SNAP recipients that year scaled to each town's own 2020-2024 five-year survey count over its mean recipients, rather than by the five-year release's town shares (which hold the 2021 Bellmont Courts and Marlridge Commons relocations for most of their span) or by SNAP shares (recipients per resident in poverty run from 0.32 to 1.15 across the towns).
stump: The default path splits the former counties' 2020-2022 estimates by the towns' shares in the 2020-2024 five-year release, which holds the 2021 Bellmont Courts and Marlridge Commons relocations for most of its span, and files Greater Ormsby $1,620,000 and Mill River Valley $2,280,000 against the golden's $1,650,000 and $2,250,000, six of the nine amounts off.
notes: Strategy grain_or_unit answered: the survey release's five-year grain and SNAP's unit (recipients, whose take-up differs by town) are both read correctly; the step is temporal disaggregation with a benchmarked indicator, which no field or rule performs. Redrawn at stage 2 from the first decisive step (midpoint anchoring of two five-year releases), whose forcing evidence the survey's sampling noise swamped; the relocations moved to 2021 at stage 3 so no published estimate displays them (Tried and rejected).
